slides.title: Chapter 5: Wallet Recovery
slides.say: Welcome to chapter five. A wallet is not a bag of coins but a bag of keys, and keys can be lost. Point at the figure from the book and ask what a person would lose if the keys vanished. By the end, one seed written as twelve words brings every key back.

slides.title: Today's route
slides.say: Seven parts follow one road, and each part opens with a divider. Point at the three counters and tell students that every code example has a twin on the course page. Ask which part they expect to be hardest. The slide numbers let anyone jump back later.
slides.takeaway: Seven parts, and at the end a backup you have actually tested.

slides.title: The questions this chapter answers
slides.say: Read the seven questions aloud and promise to return to them in the summary. Ask who can already answer the first one. Most students say a wallet holds coins, and the chapter corrects that. The check-yourself slide at the end uses the same questions.
slides.takeaway: If you can answer these seven, chapter 5 is yours.

slides.title: One chapter, eight branches
slides.say: The bars count the concepts the course page explains in each of eight branches. Point at the longest bar and ask what that branch might hold. Every concept also gets an everyday picture later in the deck. The spine of the day is keys, codes, the tree, paths and backups.
slides.takeaway: Today's spine: keys, codes, the tree, paths, backups.

slides.title: Two guesses from 7,002 bitcoin
slides.say: Tell the story slowly. Stefan Thomas was paid 7,002 bitcoin in 2011 and kept the keys on an encrypted drive. Point at the photograph and at the link, and ask what he lacked; a tested backup, not a better memory. Students often blame the drive.
slides.takeaway: Memory is not a backup; a recovery code you never test is barely one

slides.title: The tools we run today
slides.say: Every code slide uses the same small library and the same sample data. Point at the table of functions and ask which one turns words into a seed. The library is written for reading and checked against the standards' test vectors. It is not for real money.
slides.takeaway: Same library, same data, every code slide: only the idea changes.

slides.title: Part 1: Keys in wallets
slides.say: Part one asks what a wallet really holds. Point at the six concepts and read each meaning line once. Ask what the picture on the right shows; the answer is one seed and a rule give every key. A common mistake is to think that a wallet stores coins.

slides.title: What a wallet really holds
slides.say: A wallet application prepares a payment, the database supplies keys, a signing device signs, and the network receives it. Point at the four boxes in order. Ask what a wallet with public keys only can still do. It can watch funds but never spend them.
slides.takeaway: Keys are the wallet; everything else can be rebuilt from them.

slides.title: Three ways to make keys
slides.say: Compare the three pictures from the book. Independent keys need one backup each, deterministic keys need one backup, and a hierarchical wallet adds a tree on top. Point at the keys k0 to kn. Ask how many backups the third wallet needs; the answer is only one, the seed.
slides.takeaway: Independent keys: a backup for each. Seed-based keys: one backup.

slides.title: Everyday pictures for part 1
slides.say: Say the everyday picture first and the wallet meaning second. The recipe is the best one, because the ingredients are the seed, the recipe is the rule and the dish is a key. Ask students to invent their own picture for a key tweak. A key filed down by a fixed amount works.
slides.takeaway: A seed is a recipe: keep the card, and you can cook every key again.

slides.title: Code 1: Loose keys versus one seed
slides.say: Run the three boxes from top to bottom. The function key is the rule that turns the seed into key number i. Point at the table and at the True in its last row. Ask why one backup is enough; the answer is the same seed always gives the same keys.
slides.takeaway: One seed, one backup, every key.

slides.title: Part 2: Recovery codes
slides.say: Part two is about recovery codes, and a code is the seed written for human hands. Point at the six concepts and ask which one is not a recovery code; the brainwallet, because a person chose the words. Students often lump it in with the others.

slides.title: Six recovery code schemes
slides.say: Walk down the table one scheme at a time and read only the middle column. BIP39 is the common one, Electrum avoids a global word list, Aezeed carries a wallet birthday and SLIP39 splits a seed. Ask which scheme can be made by hand. Codex32.
slides.takeaway: Same goal, different trade-offs: reliability, privacy, splitting.

slides.title: Why words, and what can go wrong
slides.say: Four risks sit around a written code. Point at the card about coercion and read the number of attacks aloud. Ask why the book urges writing a code down even though words are easy to remember; the answer is memory fails and people can be forced. A brainwallet is not random.
slides.takeaway: Write it down, make it random, and do not depend on memory.

slides.title: Everyday pictures for part 2, schemes
slides.say: Seven schemes get seven everyday pictures. Point at the torn map for SLIP39, where three of five pieces show the treasure. Ask what two pieces show; the answer is nothing. Students often think two of five give a partial secret, and the picture shows why they do not.
slides.takeaway: Seven schemes, seven pictures; the torn map is the one to remember.

slides.title: Everyday pictures for part 2, choices
slides.say: A passphrase is a second lock on the safe. Point at the decoy purse and ask what plausible deniability protects against; coercion. Ask what happens when the passphrase is lost; the words alone open nothing, which is the usual surprise.
slides.takeaway: A passphrase is a second lock: lose it, and the words alone open nothing.

slides.title: Code 2: Codes check themselves differently
slides.say: Different schemes catch typos in different ways. Point at the first row of the result, codex32 valid True, and at the seed number the search found for Electrum. Ask which scheme can be checked by hand. Students are surprised that Electrum marks a seed by a prefix of an HMAC.
slides.takeaway: Every scheme has its own safety net.

slides.title: Code 3: Three of five shares recover the secret
slides.say: Secret sharing splits one secret into five shares. Point at the three rows of the result, where any three shares give True and two give False. Ask what two shares reveal; nothing at all. This is a small model and not SLIP39 itself, which works in a different field.
slides.takeaway: Any three recover; two learn nothing.

slides.title: Part 3: The BIP39 stack
slides.say: Part three follows BIP39 from random bits to a seed. Point at the six steps in the picture, from entropy to the 512-bit seed. Ask which step makes guessing slow; the answer is the stretch. A common mistake is to think the words themselves are the seed.

slides.title: Twelve words between you and 128 bits
slides.say: Tell it as a story of people. Marek Palatinus and Pavol Rusnak built the first hardware signing device and saw that nobody copies 128 bits without errors. Point at the photograph and the link to the standard. Ask why words beat bits; the answer is eleven bits fit one word.
slides.takeaway: The recovery code is an interface standard between humans and entropy

slides.title: Generating a recovery code
slides.say: Follow the five steps beside the picture, from entropy and SHA-256 to four checksum bits, twelve pieces of eleven bits and the word list. Point at the 132 bits and ask where the number comes from; 128 plus 4. Students often forget that the checksum is part of the words.
slides.takeaway: 12 words x 11 bits = 132 bits = 128 of entropy + 4 of checksum.

slides.title: Code 4: A hash function changes half its bits
slides.say: Point at the two bars, 126 bits changed and 130 unchanged. Ask what a good hash does when one letter of the input changes. About half of the output bits flip. Students expect a small change to give a small difference, and the chart shows the opposite.
slides.takeaway: A tiny change makes a huge difference.

slides.title: Code 5: How many words for how much entropy
slides.say: Point at the bars climbing in equal steps. 128 bits make 12 words and each extra 32 bits add three words. Ask how many words 256 bits need; the answer is twenty-four. The checksum grows too, by one bit for every 32 bits of entropy.
slides.takeaway: More bits, more words, more security strength.

slides.title: Code 6: From entropy to twelve words
slides.say: The chapter's own entropy becomes its own twelve words. Point at the first word, army, and its position 96. Ask why every word is just a number; eleven bits give a position from 0 to 2047 in the list. Students mix up the position with the word.
slides.takeaway: Every word is just an eleven-bit number.

slides.title: Code 7: The checksum catches a wrong word
slides.say: Decode the code back to entropy and check the last four bits. Point at the two rows and at the True and the False. Ask what the checksum catches; the answer is most typos. It cannot repair them, it only warns, and a silent typo becomes a loud error.
slides.takeaway: A checksum turns a silent typo into a loud error.

slides.title: Code 8: Text is normalised before stretching
slides.say: The same word can be stored as one character or as two. Point at the lengths 4 and 5 in the table. Ask why a phone and a laptop could disagree without normalising; the answer is they would build different seeds from the same phrase. Normalising comes before the stretch.
slides.takeaway: Normalise first, so one phrase gives one seed.

slides.title: Code 9: PBKDF2 stretches the words with a salt
slides.say: Point at the three results. One round, 2048 rounds and a changed salt give three unrelated outputs. Ask why BIP39 wants 2048 rounds; the answer is each guess becomes slower for an attacker. A different salt gives a different result, which is the same idea as a passphrase.
slides.takeaway: Slow on purpose: 2048 rounds make every guess costly.

slides.title: Code 10: A passphrase opens a different wallet
slides.say: Same twelve words, two passphrases, two wallets. Point at the two addresses and ask which one holds the funds. Only the one that was funded. This is how a decoy wallet works, and it is also how funds are lost when a passphrase is forgotten.
slides.takeaway: A passphrase is a second secret to back up.

slides.title: Everyday pictures for part 3
slides.say: Entropy is the shuffled deck, the checksum the check digit and the word list the shared dictionary. Stretching is kneading dough. Ask students which picture they remember best and why. Effort slows an attacker, which is what kneading and stretching have in common.
slides.takeaway: Shuffle, tag, name, knead: that is a recovery code.

slides.title: Everyday pictures for part 3, the book's sections
slides.say: Each section of the book gets its own picture. The padlock is the one to keep, because more entropy is a longer combination and a passphrase is a second combination on the same lock. Ask students to pair each section with its picture before you reveal the table.
slides.takeaway: More entropy is a longer combination; a passphrase is a second lock.

slides.title: Part 4: The HD wallet
slides.say: Part four builds the tree of keys. Point at the picture of how the concepts fit. One HMAC of the seed gives the master key and its chain code, and every child comes from a parent, a chain code and an index. Ask what an extended key adds; the answer is the chain code.

slides.title: One seed, a tree of keys
slides.say: The picture is the book's tree. Point at the seed, the master key m and the node m/0/1, since every node is a 32-byte key and a 32-byte chain code. Ask why the tree never runs dry; every child brings a fresh chain code. Paths are the names of the nodes.
slides.takeaway: From one seed grows a tree that backs up as one secret.

slides.title: Code 11: HMAC-SHA512 makes the master key
slides.say: HMAC-SHA512 gives 64 bytes, and the two halves are the master key and the master chain code. Point at the two halves and at the line that says True True. Ask which half is the key; the answer is the left one. Students often swap the halves.
slides.takeaway: Half of the HMAC is the key, half the chain code.

slides.title: Code 12: Child keys from a parent and an index
slides.say: Ask for children 0, 1 and 2 and look at the table, where each child gets its own key and its own chain code. Point at the two columns. Ask why the chain code is derived too; it lets the tree keep growing. Three indexes give three unrelated children.
slides.takeaway: Three indexes, three unrelated children.

slides.title: Code 13: Hardened and normal children differ
slides.say: Indexes below 2 to the 31 are normal and from there up they are hardened. Point at 2147483648 in the table. Ask what the letter h in a path means; the answer is it adds 2 to the 31 to the index. A hardened child is a different key from child 0.
slides.takeaway: The letter h in a path is a security decision.

slides.title: Code 14: Why hardened steps protect the parent
slides.say: Point at the four steps of the leak. The extended public key plus one normal child private key gives the parent private key. Ask why account levels are hardened; the answer is a hardened step cannot be undone this way. The run printed True, which is the bad news.
slides.takeaway: Normal child plus xpub exposes the parent; hardening stops it.

slides.title: Code 15: Public keys derived without private keys
slides.say: Two routes end at the same public key. Point at the box that says True. Ask how a web shop can make addresses without any private key; the answer is it derives public children from the parent public key. Students find it surprising that no secret is needed.
slides.takeaway: Public keys alone can make the shop's addresses.

slides.title: Code 16: Extended keys, xprv and xpub
slides.say: An extended key is a key plus its chain code written in Base58Check. Point at xprv and xpub, both 111 characters long. Ask which of them can spend; the answer is only xprv. The fingerprint names the key and the depth says how far down the tree it sits.
slides.takeaway: xprv can spend; xpub can only watch.

slides.title: Code 17: 2 to the 31 children, normal and hardened
slides.say: The book says 2,147,483,647 children and BIP32 says 2 to the 31. Point at the chart, two equal bars. Ask which number is the last index; the answer is 2,147,483,647, one less than the count. Students often treat the last index as the count.
slides.takeaway: The book's 2,147,483,647 is the last index, not the count.

slides.title: Everyday pictures for part 4, the tree
slides.say: The family tree fits well. The ancestor holds the master key, each child is born from a parent and a birth number, and the chain code is the family secret. Ask what keeps children unpredictable; the answer is the chain code. Let students extend the picture themselves.
slides.takeaway: A parent plus a birth number makes a child; the chain code keeps it unpredictable.

slides.title: Everyday pictures for part 4, extended keys
slides.say: An xprv is the whole archive and an xpub is a guest list that opens no doors. Point at the firewall picture for hardened derivation. Ask what a leaked child must not open; the answer is the parent. Give out the guest list, never the archive.
slides.takeaway: Give out the guest list, never the archive.

slides.title: Everyday pictures for part 4, the book's sections
slides.say: The family tree is the main picture and the others follow from it. Point at the two shelves, one for normal children and one for hardened ones. Ask which shelf protects the parent; the answer is the hardened one. Students enjoy finding the picture that fits each section.
slides.takeaway: One family tree, with a firewall for hardened children.

slides.title: Part 5: Paths and descriptors
slides.say: Part five asks which keys a wallet uses. Point at the four steps, from the recovery code to the addresses. A path names a key, standards fix common paths and a descriptor writes script and path down together. Ask what a wallet needs besides the words; the answer is the path.

slides.title: Code 18: Reading a key path level by level
slides.say: Read the path m/84h/0h/0h/1/7 level by level. Point at the five levels and at the orange ones, which are hardened. Ask which levels are normal; change and index. A common mistake is to forget that the first three levels carry an h.
slides.takeaway: Purpose, coin, account, change, index.

slides.title: Code 19: Four standard paths, four address types
slides.say: The function pub turns a path into a public key. Point at the four rows, where purposes 44, 49, 84 and 86 give four kinds of address from one recovery code. Ask which address starts with bc1p; the taproot one, purpose 86. Students expect one code to give one address.
slides.takeaway: One recovery code, four kinds of address.

slides.title: Code 20: Our address equals the standard's own
slides.say: To trust a library, compare it with a published answer. Point at the two address rows and at the True, since BIP84 prints the address and Bitcoin Core derives the same one. Ask what you would do if they differed. Stop and find the bug before using any money.
slides.takeaway: Check your code against the published vector.

slides.title: Code 21: A key tweak makes the taproot key
slides.say: A key tweak adds a number to a key and gives a related key. Point at the two 12-digit prefixes, the internal key and the output key. Ask which one the address encodes; the answer is the tweaked output key. Students expect the internal key.
slides.takeaway: Add a number to a key and you get a related key.

slides.title: Implicit and explicit paths
slides.say: Implicit paths are fixed by a standard and explicit paths are written down. Point at the last column of the table and ask why BIP49 shows coin type 1; it is the testnet type in SLIP-0044, a known quirk of the book. Write down every path that is not standard.
slides.takeaway: Know which paths are implicit and write down the rest.

slides.title: Code 22: A descriptor with its checksum and origin
slides.say: A descriptor is text that names the script and the keys. Point at the eight-character checksum and at the key origin in the bracket. Ask what the three True values mean; the answer is the first three steps are hardened. A two-of-three descriptor gets its own checksum.
slides.takeaway: One line of text can rebuild the wallet's structure.

slides.title: Multisignature, multipath and miniscript
slides.say: Multisignature, multipath and miniscript are three ways descriptors grow. Point at the picture, three keys and any two sign. Ask what a multipath descriptor saves; the answer is writing the receiving and change branches only once. Miniscript lets tools analyse a script.
slides.takeaway: Descriptors keep the wallet's rules in one line of text.

slides.title: Everyday pictures for part 5
slides.say: A path is a street address and a descriptor is the whole recipe card. Point at BIP43 and BIP44 and ask which postal rule each one is. The first number picks the scheme, and BIP44 fixes the five levels. Students often confuse the two.
slides.takeaway: A path is a street address; a descriptor is the whole recipe card.

slides.title: Everyday pictures for part 5, the book's sections
slides.say: A path is the address of one room in a building, and navigating the tree is walking down the floors. Ask what happens if you keep the key but lose its path. The key may be found but never matched to its room. Write the address down with the key.
slides.takeaway: Write the address down with the key, or the key never finds its room.

slides.title: Part 6: Data that is not keys
slides.say: Part six is about what a recovery code does not hold. Point at the four steps and ask which ones the seed cannot rebuild. Labels, protocol data and the full database. Students assume the seed restores everything, and the next slides show why it does not.

slides.title: Code 23: Labels exported in the BIP329 format
slides.say: A label names an address or a transaction. Point at the two JSON lines in the table. BIP329 stores one object per line so any program can read it. Ask what you lose if you lose the labels; the answer is your bookkeeping, not your coins.
slides.takeaway: Labels are data too: export them.

slides.title: Channels and encrypted backups
slides.say: Two answers to data that keys cannot rebuild. Point at the first picture, a static channel backup saved once, which helps but cannot guarantee results. The second picture, an encrypted wallet backup, stores everything with a key from the seed. Ask which one is made often.
slides.takeaway: Keys come back from the seed; the rest needs its own copy.

slides.title: The 200,000 BTC in a forgotten wallet file
slides.say: Tell it as a story. Mark Karpeles said on 21 March 2014 that Mt. Gox had found about 200,000 bitcoin in an old wallet file. Point at the logo and the link to The Register, and ask why nobody had checked. Backups do not expire, and an untested file is not an empty one.
slides.takeaway: Wallet files hold keys forever - label, test, and never discard them blindly

slides.title: Part 7: Deploying and testing
slides.say: Part seven puts keys to work. A shop holds only an extended public key and cold storage keeps keys offline, as the four steps show. The chapter ends with the habit that matters most, to test the backup before you need it. Ask who has ever tested one.

slides.title: Code 24: A web shop that holds no private key
slides.say: A shop makes a fresh address per customer from an extended public key. Point at the three addresses. The payment processor does this and never sees a private key. Ask what a hacked server could steal; the answer is no coins, only the list of addresses.
slides.takeaway: Publish the xpub; the keys never touch the internet.

slides.title: Code 25: The gap limit decides how far a scan looks
slides.say: Point at the chart, where gaps 5, 10 and 20 find two of the three used keys and only gap 30 finds all three. Ask why a small gap loses key 25; the scan stops after too many unused keys in a row. A scan that stops too early misses your money.
slides.takeaway: A scan that stops too early misses your money.

slides.title: Code 26: A digital signature fails if the message changes
slides.say: A signing device signs the hash of a message. Point at the two rows, True for the signed message and False for another one. Ask what a signature binds; the answer is one key to one message. This is a toy version, and you should never choose the nonce yourself in real life.
slides.takeaway: A signature binds one key to one message.

slides.title: Cold storage and the hardware signing device
slides.say: Cold storage keeps a reserve offline. Follow the four boxes in the picture, from the unsigned transaction to the signed one. Ask where the private key travels; the answer is nowhere. The written backup of the recovery code is the last line of defence, kept apart from the device.
slides.takeaway: Offline keys, a device that signs, and a code on paper.

slides.title: Code 27: The restore drill, a typo opens another wallet
slides.say: Write down the first address when the wallet is created, then point at the two rows. Restoring from the right code matches, and one wrong word gives a different, empty wallet. Ask why there is no error message; the seed function never judges the words.
slides.takeaway: Test the restore, not your luck.

slides.title: What a complete backup holds
slides.say: A complete backup is a list. Read the five items aloud and point at the test step. Ask which item people forget most often; paths and descriptors. A backup is complete only when a restore drill succeeds, not when the list is written.
slides.takeaway: A backup is complete when a restore drill succeeds.

slides.title: Everyday pictures for parts 6 and 7
slides.say: Labels are sticky notes and a static channel backup is a photocopy. The gap limit is a patient postman who stops after a set number of empty mailboxes. Ask students which part of the backup each picture reminds them of. None of these live in the seed.
slides.takeaway: Notes, copies and mailboxes: each needs its own backup or setting.

slides.title: Check yourself
slides.say: Try each question aloud before you look at the slide. If you hesitate, go back to the code slide named on the right. Ask students to pair up and quiz each other. These are the questions the exam will build on, so answer without looking.
slides.takeaway: Answer without looking, then check the code slide.

slides.title: The chapter in five lines
slides.say: Five lines carry the chapter. Read one per part and ask students to name its code slide. Wallets derive keys from a seed, a code is entropy in words, a seed is stretched slowly, the tree hands every purpose a key, and a backup counts only once restored.
slides.takeaway: If a line feels unproven, its part's code slides carry the receipt.

slides.title: Where to go from here
slides.say: These are the places to read, check and ask. Point at the Standards group and the three BIPs first. Use the tools only offline, and never type a real recovery code into a website. The course page holds the same code in the same order as the slides.
